521: Even when all property is gone, kinsmen will treat one with their usual kindness — if he has lived well by them.
522: Relatives who stay attached with unchanging love are themselves a source of ever-growing wealth.
523: Wealth that never circles among kin is like water kept in a broken pot — it never stays.
524: The whole gain of getting wealth is to live surrounded by relatives and friends.
525: Generosity and warmth draw a crowd of relatives around one.
526: No one in the world has so many kin as the one who gives largely and never yields to anger.
527: Crows call their kin to share their find before they eat. So wealth stays with those who share.
528: Relatives cluster around the leader who rewards each by merit, not alike to all.
529: Even friends who left will come back and join him, when the cause of the quarrel was not in him.
530: When one who left returns, fulfil the purpose he came back for, and receive him thoughtfully.
531: Worse than rage is the forgetfulness that comes with the drunkenness of great joy.
532: Forgetfulness destroys fame as constant poverty destroys learning.
533: Thoughtlessness never wins fame. All the treatises in the world uphold this.
534: As the coward has no defense however strong his forts, the thoughtless has no good however great his advantages.
535: The thoughtless who provides against no calamity will repent it afterward.
536: Nothing compares with unfailing thoughtfulness at all times and toward all people.
537: Nothing is too difficult, if one sets about it carefully with unflinching effort.
538: Do the things the wise have praised. Neglect them, and no happiness will come through all your births.
539: When joy lifts your mind, think of those who were ruined by neglect.
540: You can obtain anything you set your mind on — if your mind is steady enough to stay set.
541: Examine crimes, show no favor, be impartial to all, and inflict only wisely-resolved punishment.
542: As all living things thrive when the rain falls, so people thrive when the ruler judges justly.
543: A just throne upholds the scriptures and every virtue they teach.
544: The world clings to the feet of the great ruler who governs with love.
545: Rain and plentiful crops always live together in the land of the ruler who sways the sceptre justly.
546: It is not the spear that gives victory — it is the sceptre that does no injustice.
547: The ruler defends the world; and justice, administered fully, defends the ruler.
548: The ruler who gives no easy audience and no judgment on complaints will perish in disgrace.
549: The ruler's fourfold duty: guard his people from others, keep them safe himself, punish the guilty, and spare the innocent.
550: For a ruler to punish criminals with death is like pulling weeds from the green corn.
551: An oppressive ruler is crueler than a murderer on the road.
552: The unjust demand of a sceptred man is the robber's demand — a weapon in hand saying "give up your wealth."
553: The land of the ruler who does not daily hear wrongs and dispense justice falls to ruin daily.
554: The ruler who perverts justice without weighing its consequences loses wealth and people at once.
555: Will not the tears of an oppressed people become a saw that wastes their ruler's wealth away?
556: Just rule makes a ruler's fame permanent. Without it, fame does not endure.
557: As is a world without rain, so live the people whose ruler is without kindness.
558: Under an unjust ruler, being rich brings more sorrow than being poor.
559: If the ruler acts against justice, rain falls out of season and the heavens withhold their showers.
560: If the guardian guards not, the herds fail and even the learned forget their learning.
561: A true ruler examines injustice fairly and punishes so it will not be done again.
562: The ruler who wants prosperity to last should open inquiries strictly and punish mildly.
563: The cruel-sceptred ruler who rules by fear will certainly and quickly come to ruin.
564: The ruler called cruel quickly perishes — his very life grows short.
565: Wealth hoarded behind a hard face and locked doors is treasure got like a demon's.
566: The abundant wealth of the ruler with harsh words and unkind looks perishes at once instead of abiding.
567: Severe words and excessive punishments are a file that wears away a ruler's power.
568: The ruler who commits affairs to ministers without reflection, then rages at their failures, watches prosperity waste away.
569: A ruler without a fortress trembles in war and perishes quickly.
570: The earth bears no heavier burden than ignorant men whom a cruel ruler takes for his tools.
571: The world exists through that greatest ornament of rulers — a gracious presence.
572: The world's prosperity springs from kindliness. Those without it are a burden to the earth.
573: What use is a song out of tune? What use are eyes without kindliness?
574: Beyond merely sitting in the face, what do eyes do that hold no well-ordered kindness?
575: Kind looks are the eyes' ornament. Without them, they are merely two sores.
576: They are like the trees of the earth who, though they have eyes, never look kindly on others.
577: The unkind-eyed are eyeless. The truly seeing are never unkind in look.
578: The world is theirs who can show kindness without letting justice slip.
579: To bear patiently with, and show kindness to, those who grieve us — that is the most excellent of all dispositions.
580: The truly gracious stay friendly even after friends serve them poison.
581: Let a ruler count as his eyes two things: the spy and the book of laws held in universal esteem.
582: It is the ruler's duty to learn quickly all that spies can teach.
583: No ruler wins who cannot use what the spy discovers.
584: A spy watches everyone — the ruler's own employed, his relatives, and his enemies.
585: A spy is one whose appearance rouses no suspicion, who fears no man's face, and never reveals his purpose.
586: A spy takes the appearance of an ascetic, enters where he wishes, examines all, and never gives himself away, whatever is done to him.
587: A spy is one who can find out what is hidden and keep no doubt about what he has learned.
588: Let the ruler not act on a spy's report until another spy has confirmed it.
589: Employ spies who know nothing of each other. When three reports agree, receive them.
590: Never honor a spy publicly. If you do, he will divulge your own secret.
591: Energy is what makes ownership real. Without it, do we really own what we own?
592: The possession of a vigorous mind is true wealth. Wealth of money passes and does not abide.
593: Those of enduring energy will not torment themselves saying, "We have lost our property."
594: Wealth finds its own way to the one of unfailing energy.
595: As the stalks of water flowers match the depth of water, so greatness matches the mind.
596: Think greatly, and even fate cannot truly take your greatness from you.
597: The strong in mind do not faint when all is lost — the elephant stands firm under a shower of arrows.
598: Those without greatness of mind will never know the joy of saying, "We have given."
599: For all its bulk and tusks, the elephant still dreads the tiger's leap.
600: Energy is the mind's wealth. Those without it are trees in the shape of people.
601: Through the darkness of idleness, the deathless lamp of a family's name is put out.
602: Let those who want their family illustrious put away all idleness from their conduct.
603: The family of the one who acts under destructive laziness perishes before he dies.
604: Family greatness is destroyed and faults increase in those who give way to laziness and make no dignified effort.
605: Procrastination, forgetfulness, idleness, and sleep — these four are the vessel desired by those headed for destruction.
606: Rarely do the idle, though rich as kings of all the earth, gain any great benefit from it.
607: Those who let idleness keep them from worthy effort will end serving others.
608: If idleness takes up residence in a ruler of high birth, it makes him a slave of his enemies.
609: When one puts away idleness, the reproach on himself and his family disappears.
610: The ruler who never yields to laziness wins the whole earth to himself.
611: Yield not to the weakness that says "this is too hard." Effort itself gives the greatness needed to do it.
612: Never abandon work midway. The world abandons those who abandon their unfinished work.
613: The luster of generosity dwells only with the dignity of labor.
614: Generosity without work is like a sword grasped by one who cannot wield it.
615: One who desires not pleasure but labor will be a pillar to his kin, wiping away their sorrows.
616: Labor produces wealth. Idleness brings poverty.
617: They say Adversity lives with the lazy, and Fortune with the worker.
618: Adverse fate is no disgrace to anyone. To be without effort, and without knowing what should be known — that is disgrace.
620: Those who labor on, fearless and unfainting, will see even fate fall behind their back.
621: When troubles come, laugh. Nothing presses sorrow away like laughter.
622: A flood of troubles is overcome by the courageous thought the wise hold even in sorrow.
623: Sorrow itself grows sorrowful before the one who refuses to grieve.
624: Troubles themselves flee before the one who fights them head-on.
625: The troubles of that one are troubled and disappear, who however thickly they come, does not abandon his purpose.
626: Those who never clutched their wealth in good times will never cry poor in bad times.
627: The great feel no trouble as trouble — they know the body is where troubles strike.
628: Whoever seeks no pleasure and takes hardship as natural will never know sorrow.
629: Whoever never chased pleasure finds no sting in sorrow.
630: Even your enemies will honor the heights won by the one who treats pain as pleasure.
631: The minister is one who can make an excellent choice of means, time, manner of execution, and the undertaking itself.
632: Beyond these, the true minister excels in firmness and resolve.
633: The minister is one who can sow discord among foes, keep friends' goodwill, and win back those who seceded.
634: The minister is one who grasps the whole nature of a task, executes it in the best manner, and gives reassuring counsel in need.
635: He is the best helper who understands the ruler's duties and, by deep learning, gives the fullest advice at all times.
636: What scheme can stand against learning joined with natural sharpness?
637: Though you know the theoretical methods, understand the ways of the world and act accordingly.
638: However ignorant the ruler may be, it is the minister's duty to give sound advice.
639: Far better seventy crores of enemies than a minister at one's side who intends ruin.
640: The unskilled minister fails at the doing, however clever the planning.
641: Good speech is a goodness better than every other — and everyone can feel it.
642: Since both wealth and evil come from speech, ministers must guard it against every fault.
643: The minister's speech binds friends closer and makes even enemies desire his friendship.
644: Understand your hearers, then speak. Above speech there is neither virtue nor wealth.
645: Deliver your speech only after assuring yourself that no counter-speech can defeat it.
646: The flawless speak so their hearers crave more — and understand it as they hear.
647: None can conquer by intrigue the one with power of speech who is neither faulty nor timid.
648: Those who can speak on many subjects in fitting order and pleasing form — the world readily receives them.
649: They will pour out many words who do not know how to speak a few faultless ones.
650: Those who cannot set forth their learning before others are like flowers in a cluster without fragrance.
